questions.stem: Which statement best describes an Earth hazard?
options: Any natural event that has already caused deaths or damage, regardless of where or why it occurred in the past
A human activity, such as mining or farming, that changes the landscape over many years
An event that can always be prevented if enough money is spent on engineering works
An event arising from interacting Earth systems that can threaten life, health, property or the environment
questions.explanation: Earth hazards result from interactions between the geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere. Their occurrence may not be preventable, but their effects can be mitigated.

questions.stem: Earthquakes cannot be prevented. Which measure mitigates their effects?
options: Drilling deep holes along faults to let the stress escape before an earthquake
Banning all construction on bedrock, so that buildings sit only on soft sediment
Pumping concrete into active faults to stop the plates on either side moving
Building codes that require ground-shake resistant design in high-risk zones
questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces the harm a hazard causes. Building standards, land-use planning and preparedness all reduce losses, but nothing can stop plates moving or stress building on faults.

questions.stem: Why can an earthquake of the same magnitude cause far more deaths in one region than in another?
options: Building standards, population density and preparedness differ between regions
Magnitude is measured differently in each country, so the shaking is never the same
Earthquakes in some regions release no seismic waves, so their shaking is harmless
Deaths depend only on magnitude, so the difference must come from reporting errors
questions.explanation: The impact of a hazard depends on exposure and vulnerability as well as the event itself. Poorly built buildings in a crowded city turn the same shaking into a far greater disaster.

questions.stem: Where do most large earthquakes and explosive volcanic eruptions occur?
options: In the centres of continents, far from the edges of any tectonic plates
Along mid-ocean ridges, where plates move apart and the crust is thickest
Randomly over Earth's surface, with no link to the movement of plates
Along plate boundaries, especially where one plate subducts beneath another
questions.explanation: Plate tectonic processes generate most earthquakes, eruptions and tsunamis. Subduction zones produce the largest earthquakes and the most explosive volcanoes.

questions.stem: According to the elastic rebound model, how does an earthquake occur?
options: Magma rises into a fault and explodes, blasting the surrounding rock apart and releasing seismic energy
The fault slowly creeps at a steady rate, so energy is released gently and continuously
Rock at depth melts suddenly, so the ground above collapses into the space left behind
Stress builds on a locked fault, the rock bends, then ruptures and springs back, releasing energy
questions.explanation: Friction locks the fault while plate motion continues, so the rocks store elastic strain energy. When the stress exceeds the fault's strength it slips suddenly and the energy radiates as seismic waves.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake?
options: The focus is the area of worst damage; the epicentre is where the seismometer is located
The focus and epicentre are the same point, measured at different times after rupture
The focus is where rupture begins underground; the epicentre is the point on the surface above it
The epicentre is where rupture begins underground; the focus is the point on the surface above it
questions.explanation: The focus, or hypocentre, is the point within Earth where the fault starts to slip. The epicentre is directly above it on the surface.

questions.stem: Why do the largest earthquakes, of magnitude 9 or more, occur at subduction zones?
options: Subduction zones are where plates move apart fastest, tearing the crust open quickly
The plate interface is a very large locked fault that can rupture over hundreds of kilometres
Subducting plates melt completely, causing huge explosions deep inside the mantle
The crust at subduction zones is the thinnest anywhere, so the rock breaks under the least stress
questions.explanation: Magnitude depends on the area of fault that slips and how far it moves. The gently dipping megathrust between the plates can lock over an enormous area, storing energy for centuries.

questions.stem: How does the magnitude of an earthquake differ from its intensity?
options: Magnitude is the depth of the focus; intensity is the distance from the epicentre
Magnitude measures energy released at the source; intensity measures shaking effects at a place
Magnitude measures shaking effects at a place; intensity measures energy released at the source
Magnitude and intensity both measure energy, but intensity is used only for tsunamis
questions.explanation: An earthquake has one magnitude, but its intensity, described on the Modified Mercalli scale, varies from place to place with distance, depth and ground conditions.

questions.stem: On the logarithmic magnitude scale, each increase of one unit corresponds to about 32 times more energy released. About how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 5?
options: About 100 times
About 1000 times
About 2 times
About 64 times
questions.explanation: Two units means 32 × 32 ≈ 1000 times the energy. The ground motion amplitude is 10 × 10 = 100 times larger, which is a common source of confusion.

questions.stem: At a seismograph station, the S waves from an earthquake arrive some seconds after the P waves. Why does this gap increase with distance from the earthquake?
options: Both waves travel at the same speed, but S waves start later at the focus
S waves slow down only when they reach the station's soft sediments
P waves travel faster than S waves, so the further they go the more they pull ahead
S waves travel faster than P waves, but they take a longer path through the core
questions.explanation: Both waves leave the focus together, but P waves are faster. The longer the journey, the greater the time between their arrivals, so the S-P interval gives the distance to the earthquake.

questions.stem: Why are records from at least three seismograph stations needed to locate an earthquake's epicentre?
options: Each gives only a distance, so circles from three stations are needed to meet at one point
Each gives only a direction, so three bearings are averaged to find the epicentre
Each records only one wave type, so three stations are needed to record P, S and surface waves
Each measures the magnitude differently, so three readings are averaged to find the location
questions.explanation: One station's S-P interval gives a circle of possible epicentres. Two circles cross at two points, and a third circle identifies which point is the epicentre.

questions.stem: The 1968 Meckering earthquake in Western Australia occurred far from any plate boundary. Which explanation best fits?
options: A mantle plume rose beneath Meckering and broke the continental crust open as a new spreading ridge
A subduction zone lies directly beneath the Wheatbelt, where an ocean plate is sinking
The earthquake was caused by the weight of farm dams pressing down on the crust
Stress transmitted through the Australian plate from its boundaries reactivated a fault in the interior
questions.explanation: Intraplate earthquakes happen because forces at plate boundaries compress the whole plate. Ancient faults in the interior can slip when this stress builds, even though they are far from a boundary.

questions.stem: The explosivity of a volcanic eruption depends mainly on the magma's:
options: iron content, which controls its colour, and the age of the volcano itself
temperature alone, since hotter magma is always more explosive
distance from the ocean, since seawater causes every explosion
silica content, which controls viscosity, and the amount of dissolved gas
questions.explanation: High-silica magma is viscous, so dissolved gases cannot escape easily. Pressure builds until the magma fragments explosively. Hotter basaltic magma is usually less explosive, not more.

questions.stem: Compared with rhyolitic magma, basaltic magma usually erupts as lava flows rather than explosively because it:
options: has low silica and low viscosity, so gas escapes easily as it rises
has high silica and high viscosity, so gas is trapped until it cools
contains no dissolved gas at all, since it forms from melted crust
is cooler than rhyolitic magma, so it cannot build up any pressure
questions.explanation: Basaltic magma has about 45 to 52% silica and is hot and runny, so bubbles escape gently, producing lava flows and shield volcanoes. Rhyolitic magma is cooler, silica-rich and viscous.

questions.stem: Why are volcanoes above subduction zones often explosive?
options: Subduction zone magma comes straight from the outer core and is extremely hot
Water from the sinking slab helps form gas-rich magma of intermediate silica content
The sinking slab cools the mantle, so the magma has very low silica and very low gas content
Seawater pours directly into the magma chamber through cracks in the ocean floor
questions.explanation: Water released from the subducting plate lowers the melting point of the mantle above it. The resulting magma becomes more silica-rich as it rises through the crust, and its water becomes gas that drives explosive eruptions.

questions.stem: Magma A has 50% silica and is at 1150 °C. Magma B has 72% silica and is at 800 °C. Which prediction is best supported?
options: B is more likely to erupt explosively with pyroclastic flows; A is more likely to form lava flows
A is more likely to erupt explosively with pyroclastic flows; B is more likely to form lava flows
Both are equally explosive, because explosivity depends only on the volume of magma
Neither can erupt, because magma below 1200 °C has already solidified completely
questions.explanation: Higher silica and lower temperature make magma B far more viscous, trapping gas and favouring explosive eruptions, while hot, low-silica magma A behaves like basalt. Magma composition is therefore used to predict the degree of explosivity.

questions.stem: A pyroclastic flow is:
options: a cloud of fine ash that drifts high in the stratosphere for several years
a mudflow of volcanic ash and water that flows down the river valleys after heavy rain
a fast-moving avalanche of hot gas, ash and rock fragments that races down a volcano
a slow-moving stream of runny basaltic lava that can be outrun on foot
questions.explanation: Pyroclastic flows can travel at well over 100 km/h at hundreds of degrees, destroying everything in their path. A mudflow of ash and water is a lahar.

questions.stem: Why can lahars threaten towns many kilometres from a volcano, even years after an eruption?
options: Lava stays molten underground for years and erupts again from distant river beds
Volcanic gases build up in the valleys and explode when they finally reach towns downstream
Ash in the stratosphere falls as hot rocks onto distant towns for many years
Loose ash on the slopes can be mobilised by heavy rain and flow far down river valleys
questions.explanation: A lahar is a mudflow of volcanic debris and water. Rain, melting snow or a breached crater lake can turn loose ash into a fast, concrete-like flow that follows valleys for long distances.

questions.stem: After a large explosive eruption, global average temperatures may fall slightly for a year or two. Why?
options: Carbon dioxide from the eruption absorbs infrared radiation and so cools Earth's surface
Lava flows cover large areas, increasing the albedo of the whole planet's surface
Ash particles absorb all the heat emitted by Earth and carry it out into space
Sulfur dioxide forms sulfate aerosols in the stratosphere that reflect incoming sunlight
questions.explanation: Sulfur gases injected into the stratosphere form tiny droplets that reflect sunlight back to space, cooling the surface. This shows how volcanic emissions affect climate and weather.

questions.stem: Why does a large eruption cause only brief cooling, and why must its sulfur reach the stratosphere to affect global climate?
options: Tropospheric aerosols rain out in weeks, while stratospheric aerosols spread globally but settle in a few years
Tropospheric aerosols spread globally for decades, while stratospheric aerosols fall out within days
Sulfur in the troposphere warms the climate strongly, so only stratospheric sulfur can cause any cooling at all
Sulfur stays in the stratosphere permanently, so the cooling lasts until the next eruption occurs
questions.explanation: Rain quickly washes aerosols out of the lower atmosphere. In the stratosphere there is no rain, so aerosols spread around the globe, but they still settle out over one to three years, so the cooling is temporary.

questions.stem: Which monitoring observation most strongly suggests magma is rising beneath a volcano?
options: A steady decrease in the number of earthquakes beneath the volcano
A fall in the amount of sulfur dioxide escaping from the crater
A gradual subsidence of the volcano's summit over several years
A swarm of small earthquakes becoming more frequent and shallower
questions.explanation: Rising magma fractures the rock around it, producing swarms of small earthquakes that move closer to the surface. Increasing gas output and swelling of the ground often accompany them.

questions.stem: Tiltmeters and GPS stations on a volcano record its flanks bulging outward over several weeks. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The magma chamber is emptying, so the volcano's flanks are collapsing inward
Groundwater is being pumped from beneath the volcano by nearby farms
The volcano is cooling and contracting, so an eruption is unlikely
Magma is accumulating in a chamber beneath the volcano, inflating the ground
questions.explanation: Ground deformation monitoring detects inflation as magma or gas pressure builds below. Deflation would suggest the chamber is losing magma or pressure.

questions.stem: At a volcano, earthquakes are increasing and becoming shallower, the summit is inflating, and sulfur dioxide emissions have doubled. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Raise the alert level and prepare to evacuate the zones shown as high risk on the hazard map
Lower the alert level, since rising gas output means the pressure in the magma body is now falling
Wait for lava to appear at the surface, since monitoring data cannot indicate an eruption
Evacuate only the summit area, since volcanic hazards never extend beyond the crater
questions.explanation: Several independent signals together suggest fresh magma rising towards the surface. Monitoring cannot give an exact time, but combined data justify raising the alert and preparing to move people out of hazard zones.

questions.stem: On a hazard map of a stratovolcano, river valleys draining its slopes are shaded as high risk even many kilometres away. Why?
options: Valleys are where ash falls most thickly, because ash is heavier than the air
Lahars and pyroclastic flows are channelled along valleys, as past deposits show
Valleys are always closest to the magma chamber, so lava erupts from them first
Valleys collect earthquake waves, so they shake more than any ridge or summit
questions.explanation: Hazard maps are built from the distribution of past deposits and from modelling. Dense flows of ash, rock and water follow topography, so valleys funnel them far from the volcano.

questions.stem: Seismologists plot the epicentres of thousands of earthquakes recorded over several decades. How does this help reduce earthquake risk?
options: It shows the active faults and plate boundaries, so hazard zones can be mapped
It shows the exact date of the next earthquake on each fault in the region
It shows where earthquakes have stopped forever, so building there is safe
It replaces the need for building codes in areas without past earthquakes
questions.explanation: Earthquake location and frequency data reveal where seismic hazard is concentrated. This supports hazard maps, building codes and planning, even though the timing of individual earthquakes cannot be predicted.

questions.stem: Trenches across a fault show that six large earthquakes occurred on it in the last 1500 years. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The fault ruptures exactly every 250 years, so the next date can be predicted precisely
The average recurrence interval is about 9000 years, so the fault is effectively inactive
Each earthquake releases all stress permanently, so there will be no more large earthquakes
The average recurrence interval is about 250 years, but the next could come sooner or later
questions.explanation: 1500 ÷ 6 = 250 years on average. Recurrence data give the probability of repeat events, not an exact schedule, because the intervals between earthquakes vary.

questions.stem: Along an active plate boundary, one segment has had no large earthquake for over a century while the segments on either side have ruptured. Why is this seismic gap considered high risk?
options: The segment is made of molten rock, which cannot produce earthquakes
The segment absorbed the energy of its neighbours, which made it safe
Stress has kept building on that segment, so it is likely to rupture in future
The segment has stopped moving, so stress there has been released for good
questions.explanation: Plate motion loads the whole boundary. A segment that has not slipped has accumulated strain, so it is considered more likely to produce a large earthquake.

questions.stem: Most large tsunamis are generated by:
options: small earthquakes on faults where plates slide sideways past each other
sudden vertical movement of the sea floor during large subduction earthquakes
strong onshore winds blowing for several days during a tropical cyclone
the daily rise and fall of the tides caused by the Moon's gravitational pull
questions.explanation: When a megathrust ruptures, the sea floor is pushed up or dropped over a large area, displacing the whole water column. Landslides and volcanic collapses can also cause tsunamis. Strike-slip faults move mainly sideways, so they rarely displace much water.

questions.stem: How does a tsunami change as it moves from the deep ocean into shallow coastal water?
options: It slows down and its height decreases, so it is harmless on arrival
It slows down and its height increases greatly as the water shallows
It speeds up and its height decreases as the water becomes shallower
It keeps the same speed and height until it breaks on the beach
questions.explanation: In deep water a tsunami travels very fast with a height of perhaps a metre or less. As the depth decreases it slows and the wave energy is squeezed into less water, so the wave grows much taller.

questions.stem: A tsunami's speed in the open ocean is given by v = √(g × d). Using g = 10 m/s², how long would a tsunami take to cross 1440 km of ocean 4000 m deep?
options: About 2 hours
About 7 minutes
About 20 minutes
About 12 hours
questions.explanation: v = √(10 × 4000) = √40 000 = 200 m/s. Time = 1 440 000 m ÷ 200 m/s = 7200 s, which is 2 hours. Dividing 1440 km by 200 without converting units gives 7.2, a common slip.

questions.stem: Tsunami warning systems use both seismometers and deep-ocean pressure sensors. Why are the pressure sensors needed as well?
options: Pressure sensors measure the earthquake's magnitude, which seismometers cannot do
Pressure sensors stop the tsunami wave before it reaches the continental shelf
Seismometers detect the earthquake quickly, but sensors confirm whether a tsunami formed
Seismometers cannot detect earthquakes beneath the sea floor, so the sensors are the only source
questions.explanation: Not every undersea earthquake produces a tsunami. Seismic data give an early alert, and sea-floor pressure sensors detect the passing wave, confirming the threat and its size.

questions.stem: Which source poses the main tsunami threat to Western Australia's north-west coast?
options: Earthquakes on the subduction zone along the Indonesian arc
Earthquakes on the mid-ocean ridge in the central Atlantic
Eruptions of the volcanoes in the Southern Alps of New Zealand
Tropical cyclones forming over the Coral Sea in summer
questions.explanation: The Indo-Australian plate subducts beneath the Indonesian arc, the nearest major subduction zone to Western Australia. Tsunamis generated there have reached the State's north-west coast.

questions.stem: People on a beach notice the sea suddenly withdraw far below the low-tide mark. What should they do?
options: Move immediately to high ground or well inland, because a tsunami may follow
Walk out onto the exposed sea floor to collect stranded fish and shells
Wait on the beach to watch, because the water will return slowly over hours
Shelter behind beach dunes, because waves cannot cross even low sand ridges
questions.explanation: A sudden withdrawal can mean the trough of a tsunami has arrived first, and the crest may follow within minutes. Natural warning signs should be acted on without waiting for an official warning.

questions.stem: During strong shaking, buildings on loose, water-saturated sand tilt and sink, and sand bubbles up through cracks. What has happened?
options: Weathering: the sand broke down chemically into clay during the shaking
Liquefaction: the sand temporarily lost its strength and behaved like a liquid
Subduction: the sand was dragged down into the mantle beneath the building
Lithification: the sand was cemented into sandstone by the shaking
questions.explanation: Shaking raises the water pressure between grains, so they lose contact and the ground flows. The structure and composition of Earth materials strongly influence earthquake damage.

questions.stem: Two towns are the same distance from an earthquake's epicentre. Town P is built on solid granite; town Q is built on thick, soft, water-saturated sediment. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Both suffer identical damage, because they are the same distance from the epicentre
Neither is damaged, because surface waves cannot travel through either material
Q suffers more damage, because soft sediment amplifies shaking and may liquefy
P suffers more damage, because granite transmits shaking but sediment absorbs it
questions.explanation: Seismic waves slow down and grow in amplitude in soft sediments, and saturated sediment can liquefy. Hard rock shakes less, so the impact depends on Earth materials as well as distance.

questions.stem: A magnitude 6.0 earthquake with a focus 10 km below a city causes heavy damage. A magnitude 8.0 earthquake 600 km below a remote region causes little. Which statement best explains this?
options: The magnitude 6.0 earthquake released more energy, because magnitude is measured at depth
Deep earthquakes produce no seismic waves, so the magnitude 8.0 caused no shaking at all
The magnitude scale is reversed, so lower numbers indicate more powerful earthquakes
Impact depends on location and intensity: shallow shaking near people is most destructive
questions.explanation: The magnitude 8.0 released about 1000 times more energy, but waves from a deep focus weaken before reaching the surface, and few people lived nearby. Shallow focus beneath a city gives high intensity where exposure is greatest.

questions.stem: Which design feature helps a building resist ground shaking?
options: Heavy unreinforced brick walls that add extra weight to hold the building firmly in place
A rigid, brittle concrete frame that cannot bend at all when the ground moves
Extra storeys added to the roof to keep the building's centre of gravity high
Base isolators that let the ground move beneath the building without shaking it as much
questions.explanation: Advances in understanding seismic processes have led to designs that absorb or isolate shaking, such as base isolation, cross-bracing and ductile frames. Unreinforced masonry is among the most dangerous construction in earthquakes.

questions.stem: Some ecosystems rely on episodic hazard events. How do floods help maintain the fertility of a river's floodplain?
options: Floodwaters add salt to the soil, which most floodplain plants require
Floodwaters remove all seeds, so only introduced plants can establish
Floodwaters spread fine, nutrient-rich sediment across the floodplain soil
Floodwaters wash away all the soil, exposing fresh bedrock for plants
questions.explanation: Silt and organic matter dropped by floodwaters renew soil nutrients, and flooding triggers breeding and germination in many floodplain species. The hazard is part of the system's long-term viability.

questions.stem: Many banksia species in Western Australia hold their seeds in woody cones that open mainly after fire. Why is this an advantage?
options: Fire adds water to the soil, which seeds need to break out of their cones
Seeds are released onto cleared, ash-enriched ground with little competition
Fire kills all the insects that would otherwise eat the banksia flowers
Seeds released before a fire would germinate in the flames and grow faster
questions.explanation: After a fire the ground is open and fertilised by ash, giving seedlings light, nutrients and space. Bushfire therefore helps rejuvenate and maintain these ecosystems.

questions.stem: How can detailed models of plate tectonic motion help a region make local decisions?
options: They predict the exact day of each future earthquake, so that buildings can be evacuated well in advance
They stop plate movement in high-risk areas by showing engineers where to reinforce the crust
They show that all regions have equal hazard, so the same building rules can apply everywhere
They identify areas of high seismic hazard and high heat flow, guiding building and geothermal siting
questions.explanation: Models of plate motion and collision inform evidence-based decisions about where and how to build infrastructure and where geothermal resources are likely. They give probabilities and patterns, not exact timings.
